passages.context: Bellarmine reads the opening cry in the person of Christ on the cross, asking to be heard in a speedy resurrection, and returns at verse 7 to God's help, the heart's confidence, Christ's flourishing flesh, and praise after victory. He then extends the closing petition from Christ the glorified head to the people acquired by his blood.

passages.context: Bellarmine first reads David's exaltation and healing in his deliverance and kingship, then reads the same speech prophetically in Christ and in the elect: abasement gives way to resurrection, immortality, and the heavenly kingdom. His explanation of the cry and healing joins literal deliverance from danger to Christ's rising and the saints' final salvation.

passages.context: Bellarmine places David's trust amid his flight from Absalom and the conspiracy at Jerusalem. He explains 'Thou art my God' as confidence in the all-powerful protector, and 'My lots are in thy hands' as the confession that life depends not on lot or chance but on God's will and power, followed by the prayer for deliverance from persecutors.

passages.context: Bellarmine reads the Psalm through Christ's resurrection, ascension, and the establishment of the Church. At the clauses used by the proper he emphasizes God's special care for orphans, widows, the oppressed, and the poor in spirit; the Holy Ghost's work of bringing persons of one mind into one house and freeing those bound in sin; and God's final wonder in raising the saints and giving his people immortality, power, and strength.

passages.context: Bellarmine's whole treatment is one compressed paragraph aimed at the liturgical fact: a verse celebrated in the Catholic Church, as all the divine offices commence with it; peculiarly applicable to Christ hanging on the cross yet usable by all the faithful in any danger whatever; and the remainder of the psalm almost word for word with Psalm 39, which see - the doublet stated plainly. Later Christian reception of the Introit's verse-pair.

passages.context: Bellarmine places the lament principally under Antiochus Epiphanes and the Maccabean persecution, while explaining that the opening question does not assert a fixed divine rejection. The closing petitions call cruel persecutors beasts, invoke the covenant and the oppressed people, make the people's cause God's own because the reproach falls upon him, and ask that the enemies' continuing pride not pass unpunished.

passages.context: Bellarmine treats the opening summons as cheerful praise flowing from love and desire, directed to God the helper and God of Jacob. He receives the psalm, timbrel, psaltery, harp, and trumpet as the appointed instruments of solemn thanksgiving, commanded in Israel so that God's benefits, especially deliverance from Egypt, remain in memory.

passages.context: Bellarmine reads the psalm of one under grievous affliction as agreeing to Christ in his Passion, and concretizes the Alleluia verse's day and night into Good Friday and Gethsemane: he did so on the day of his passion, when he cried on the cross, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? and on the night before, when he thrice cried out in the garden. Later Christian reception of the Alleluia's verse.

passages.context: Bellarmine receives the opening address as grateful recollection before fresh petition: amid many dangers, God's people have found in him not occasional shelter but a secure refuge from generation to generation. He develops that refuge as continual dwelling in God through faith, hope, charity, recollection, and desire.

passages.context: Bellarmine reads the Communion's verses literally and providentially - bread taken for the food of man in general, wine may cheer the heart of man intelligible enough - and draws three morals: God the source of all supports and enjoyments of corporal life; the fond Father who gave even the luxuries; and the duty of frugal meals and moderate drink. The tradition's literal pole beside Augustine's christological and Cassiodorus's sacramental readings.

work.author: Robert Bellarmine
work.description: Bellarmine's verse-by-verse exposition of the Psalms. The 1866 English expression is materially abridged by its translator, who says that he omitted philological discussion, variant readings, and Bellarmine's individual Psalm prefaces; claims drawn from that expression must not be represented as controlling the complete Latin work.
